source_text: Paulus vero Apostolus de persecutore, qui primus Ecclesiae sanguinem fudit, postea gladium stylo mutans, et convertens machaeram in aratrum; lupus rapax Benjamin, dehinc ipse afferens escam secundum Jacob, qualiter martyria, jam et sibi optabilia, commendat! cum de Thessalonicensibus gaudens: Uti, inquit, gloriemur in vobis in Ecclesiis Dei pro tolerantia vestra et fide, in omnibus persecutionibus et pressuris, quibus sustinetis ostentamen justi judicii Dei, ut digni habeamini regno ejus, pro quo et patimini. Sicut et ad Romanos: Non solum autem, verum etiam exultantes in pressuris; certi quod pressura tolerantiam perficit, tolerantia vero probationem, probatio autem spem, spes vero non confundit. Et rursus: Quod si filii, et haeredes; haeredes quidem Dei, cohaeredes vero Christi: siquidem compatimur, uti et cum illo glorificemur. Reputo enim passiones hujus temporis non esse dignas ad gloriam, quae in nobis revelabitur. Et ideo postmodum: Quis, inquit, separabit nos a dilectione Christi? pressura, an angustia, an fames, an nuditas, an periculum, an machaera, secundum quod scriptum est: tui caussa mortificamur tota die, deputati sumus ut pecora jugulationis; sed in omnibus istis supervincimus pro eo qui nos dilexit. Persuasum enim habemus, quod neque mors, neque vita, neque virtus, neque sublimitas, neque profundum, neque alia conditio poterit nos a dilectione Dei separare, quae est in Christo Jesu Domino nostro. Sed et Corinthiis passiones suas enumerans, patiendum utique praefinivit: In laboribus abundantius, in carceribus plurimum, in mortibus saepius; a Judaeis quinquies quadragenas citra unam accepi, ter virgis caesus, semel lapidatus, et reliqua. Quae si magis incommoda quam martyria videbuntur, tamen rursus: Propter quod, inquit, boni duco in infirmitatibus, in injuriis, in necessitatibus, in persecutionibus, in angustiis pro Christo. Etiam in superioribus: Qui in omnibus tribulemur, sed non coangustemur; et indigeamus, sed non perindigeamus; quoniam persecutionibus agitemur, sed non derelinquamur; qui dejiciamur, sed non pereamus: semper mortificationem Christi Jesu in corpore nostro circumferentes. Sed etsi, inquit, exterior homo noster vitiatur, caro scilicet, vi persecutionum; sed interior renovatur die et die; anima scilicet spe promissionum. Nam quod ad praesens, temporale et leve pressurae nostrae per supergressum in supergressum aeternum pondus gloriae perficit nobis, non intuentibus quae videntur, sed quae non videntur. Quae enim videntur, temporalia, de incommodis dicens; quae vero non videntur, aeterna, de praemiis spondens. Thessalonicensibus vero de vinculis scribens, utique beatos affirmavit,, quibus donatum esset non tantum credere in Christum, sed etiam pro ipso pati: Eumdem, inquit, agonem habentes quem in me vidistis, et nunc audistis. Nam et si libor super sacrificium, gaudeo et congaudeo omnibus vobis, perinde et vos gaudete et congaudete mihi. Vides quam martyrii definiat felicitatem, cui de gaudio mutuo acquirit solemnitatem. Ut proximus denique voti sui factus est, qualiter de prospectu ejus exsultans Timotheo scribit? Ego enim jam libor, et tempus dijunctionis instat. Agonem bonum decertavi, cursum consummavi, fidem custodivi; superest corona, quam mihi Dominus illa die reddet, scilicet passionis. Satis et ipse supra allocutus: Fidelis sermo: si enim commortui sumus Christo, et convivemus; si sufferimus, et conregnabimus; si negaverimus, et ille nos negabit; si non credimus, ille fidelis est, negare se non potest. Ne ergo confundaris martyrio Domini nostri, neque me vinctum ejus; quia praedixerat: Non enim dedit nobis Deus spiritum timoris, sed virtutis et dilectionis et sanae mentis. Virtute enim patimur ex dilectione in Deum, et sana mente, cum ob innocentiam patimur. Sed et sicubi tolerantiam praecipit, quibus magis eam quam passionibus prospicit? sicubi ab idololatria divellit, quid ei magis quam martyria praevellit?
pass_a_gloss: Paul, Apostle, indeed, about persecutor, who first poured out Church's blood, afterwards changing sword with stylus, and converting machete into plow; rapacious wolf Benjamin, then himself bringing food according to Jacob, how martyrdoms, now even desirable to him, he commends! when rejoicing about Thessalonians: We glory, he says, in you in Churches of God for your endurance and faith, in all persecutions and pressures, which you endure, a demonstration of God's just judgment, so that you may be considered worthy of His kingdom, for which you also suffer. Just as also to Romans: Not only, but also rejoicing in pressures; certain that pressure perfects endurance, endurance truly probation, probation indeed hope, hope indeed does not disappoint. And again: If we are sons, and heirs; heirs indeed of God, coheirs truly of Christ: if we suffer, so that we may also be glorified with Him. I consider that passions of this time are not worthy of glory, which will be revealed in us. And therefore afterwards: Who, he says, will separate us from love of Christ? pressure, or distress, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger, or sword, according to what is written: for Your sake we are killed all day, we are considered as sheep for slaughter; but in all these things we overcome on account of Him who loved us. For we are persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor virtue, nor height, nor depth, nor any other condition can separate us from love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord. But also to Corinthians, enumerating his own passions, he certainly defined suffering: In labors more abundantly, in prisons very much, in deaths often; from Jews I received forty lashes minus one five times, three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, and the rest. Which if they seem more inconveniences than martyrdoms, nevertheless again: On account of which, he says, I consider them good in weaknesses, in injuries, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ. Also in the preceding: Who in all things are troubled, but not constrained; and we are in need, but not in extreme need; since we are persecuted, but not abandoned; who are cast down, but not perishing: always carrying about death of Christ Jesus in our body. But if, he says, our outer man is being destroyed, namely the flesh, by means of persecutions; but our inner man is being renewed day by day; namely the soul by means of hope of promises. For what is present, temporal and light pressure of ours is producing for us, by surpassing, eternal weight of glory, not looking at what is seen, but what is not seen. For what is seen is temporal, speaking about inconveniences; what is not seen is eternal, promising about rewards. To Thessalonians indeed, writing about chains, he certainly affirmed that those are blessed to whom it has been given not only to believe in Christ, but also to suffer for Him: Having, he says, the same struggle which you saw in me and now hear. For even if I am poured out as a sacrifice, I rejoice and congratulate all of you, and you rejoice and congratulate me in like manner. You see how he defines happiness of martyrdom, by which he acquires solemnity from mutual joy. So that, having become next to his own wish, how he writes to Timothy, exulting from his own prospect? For I am already being poured out, and time of departure is at hand. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; there remains a crown, which the Lord will give me on that day, namely of passion. Having spoken sufficiently above: Faithful is the word: if we have died with Christ, and we live; if we suffer, and we will reign; if we deny, and He will deny us; if we do not believe, He is faithful, He cannot deny Himself. So do not be ashamed of martyrdom of our Lord, nor of me, bound for Him; because He predicted: For God did not give us a spirit of fear, but of power and love and sound mind. For we suffer with power from love for God, and with sound mind, when we suffer on account of innocence. But also where he commands endurance, to whom does he foresee it more than to those who suffer martyrdoms? where he tears them away from idolatry, what does he tear them away more than martyrdoms?

pass_b_english: Paul, the Apostle, has a remarkable story to tell - from being a persecutor who shed the Church's blood to becoming a champion of the faith, trading his sword for a pen and turning his destructive ways into constructive ones, just like the rapacious wolf Benjamin, who later brought food to the table, as Jacob had said. Now, Paul commends martyrdom, even considering it desirable, as he writes to the Thessalonians, rejoicing in their endurance and faith in the face of persecution, which demonstrates God's just judgment and makes them worthy of His kingdom (2 Timothy 4:7-8).

Paul's message to the Romans is just as striking: not only do they endure pressure, but they also rejoice in it, knowing that it perfects their endurance, which in turn leads to hope, and hope never disappoints. As he puts it, if we're sons and daughters of God, and heirs of His kingdom, coheirs with Christ, then we'll suffer with Him, but also be glorified with Him. Paul believes that the struggles of this life are nothing compared to the glory that will be revealed in us, and he's convinced that nothing - not even death, life, virtue, or any other circumstance - can separate us from God's love, which is found in Christ Jesus our Lord (Romans 8:35-39).

Paul shares his own experiences with the Corinthians, listing his many struggles, from labors and imprisonments to beatings and stonings, and yet he considers these struggles good, even desirable, because they're a testament to his love for Christ. He says that even when we're troubled, we're not crushed; when we're in need, we're not in despair; when we're persecuted, we're not abandoned. Instead, we carry the death of Christ Jesus in our bodies, and our inner selves are renewed day by day, thanks to the hope of promises. Paul believes that our present struggles, though temporal and fleeting, will produce an eternal weight of glory, and that's what matters - not what we see, but what we don't see (2 Corinthians 4:10).

Writing to the Thessalonians from prison, Paul affirms that those who believe in Christ and suffer for Him are truly blessed. He shares his own struggles, and yet he rejoices and congratulates the Thessalonians, inviting them to rejoice with him. For Paul, the happiness of martyrdom is rooted in mutual joy, and he's willing to be poured out as a sacrifice for the sake of Christ. As he writes to Timothy, he's confident that he's fought the good fight, finished the course, and kept the faith, and he looks forward to receiving a crown from the Lord on the day of his passion. Paul's message is clear: don't be ashamed of the martyrdom of our Lord, or of those who suffer for Him, because God has given us a spirit of power, love, and sound mind, not fear. We suffer with power and love, and with a sound mind, when we're persecuted for our innocence, and that's what Paul wants us to remember.

review.notes: Pass B is a paraphrase/summary rather than a translation, failing the completeness requirement for a translation task. Specifically, Pass B omits the detailed list of Paul's sufferings (the 'forty lashes minus one five times, three times beaten with rods, once stoned' from the Latin: 'a Judaeis quinquies quadragenas citra unam accepi, ter virgis caesus, semel lapidatus') and the specific theological distinction regarding the 'outer man' and 'inner man' (Pass A: 'exterior homo noster vitiatur... sed interior renovatur'). Furthermore, Pass B adds interpretive flourishes not present in the Latin, such as 'remarkable story to tell' and 'champion of the faith'.
reasons: Pass B is a summary/paraphrase that omits significant portions of the source text, such as the specific enumeration of Paul's physical sufferings ('a Judaeis quinquies quadragenas citra unam accepi, ter virgis caesus, semel lapidatus') and the distinction between the outer and inner man ('exterior homo noster vitiatur... sed interior renovatur').
